newsitem.title: USA: FTC parts curtain slightly on merger secrecy.
newsitem.headline: FTC parts curtain slightly on merger secrecy.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission parted the curtain of secrecy surrounding its antitrust reviews by a few inches Friday, announcing it will make public the names involved in some merger reviews.
Beginning next week, the FTC will disclose it is investigating a proposed merger if a party to the transaction has announced it to the press or made a public government filing.
Until now, the FTC has refused to acknowledge it is investigating particular companies in a merger, even if the companies trumpet the news.

One example would be the proposed merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell-Douglas Corp.. The FTC has never acknowledged publicly that it is looking into that merger, although it was announced by the CEOs of both firms.
In a statement, the FTC noted that its new policy is similar to one already followed at the antitrust division of the Department of Justice.
Although the commission vote in favour of the new policy was 5-0, Commissioner Mary Azcuenaga dissented in part.
She said she was "dissenting to the extent we didn't put it out for public comment."

She said the commission was informed that businesses had no objection. But she noted that the old policy had lasted for many years -- it was last reaffirmed in 1977 -- and said businesses should have had a 30-day comment period to raise any rational objections.

James Love, of Ralph Nader's Consumer Project on Technology, had suggested the change. He applauded the move and said it would "permit ordinary citizens to more fully participate in the merger review process."
He said the change would also pave the way for the FTC to list individual cases for comment on its Web page, should it choose to do so.
